## Report: Abortion and Breast Cancer Risk

**Conclusion:** The current scientific consensus does not support the claim that having an abortion increases a woman's risk of breast cancer.

**Evidence:**

The National Cancer Institute (NCI) convened a workshop of over 100 leading experts in 2003 to review population-based, clinical, and animal studies on pregnancy and breast cancer risk. The workshop concluded that abortion does not increase a woman's risk of breast cancer, and the NCI posted a revised fact sheet reflecting this conclusion (https://www.cancer.gov/types/breast/abortion-miscarriage-risk).

The American Cancer Society states that "the scientific evidence does not support the notion that abortion of any kind raises the risk of breast cancer or any other type of cancer" (https://www.theatlantic.com/national/2013/12/inside-faulty-science-abortion-breast-cancer-link/355850/). Their most recent information confirms that "abortion does not influence a woman's risk for breast cancer" (https://www.cancer.org/cancer/risk-prevention/medical-treatments/abortion-and-breast-cancer-risk.html).

The Collaborative Group on Hormonal Factors in Breast Cancer conducted a major collaborative reanalysis of data from 53 epidemiological studies, including 83,000 women with breast cancer from 16 countries. This large-scale analysis found no overall association between induced abortion and breast cancer risk (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0140673604158352).

**Context:** Some older case-control studies and advocacy groups have claimed a link, but these studies are susceptible to recall bias. Larger prospective studies and meta-analyses have not confirmed this association. A 2018 updated meta-analysis noted that "prospective evidences did not support the positive association" (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29504989/?dopt=Abstract).

The claim appears to originate from selective interpretation of older studies, but the weight of current scientific evidence does not support it.
